topic: Increase in Supreme Court Judge Strength

subtopics.title: Expansion Bill and Legal Framework
subtopics.summary: The Union Cabinet approved the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill 2026 to expand the Court to 38 judges, which is the Chief Justice plus 37 other judges. Article 124 empowers Parliament to change the number of judges by law, and the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Act, 1956 governs this. The Court was inaugurated in 1950 and succeeded the Federal Court of India.
facts: Cabinet approved the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill 2026
Proposed strength is 38 judges (CJI plus 37 other judges)
Article 124 empowers Parliament to increase judges by law
Governed by the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Act, 1956
Increase needs an Amendment Bill passed by both Houses
Simple majority is sufficient; Presidential assent is also needed
Inaugurated on 28 January 1950
Succeeded the Federal Court of India (Government of India Act, 1935)
Replaced the British Privy Council as the highest court of appeal
Originally fixed at 8 (Chief Justice and 7 other judges)

subtopics.title: Qualifications, Tenure and Removal
subtopics.summary: Judges of the Supreme Court are appointed by the President, subject to qualifications set in the Constitution. A judge holds office until the age of 65 and may resign by writing to the President. Removal is only on grounds of proven misbehaviour or incapacity, under the Judges Enquiry Act, 1968, and needs a Parliamentary vote.
facts: Judges are appointed by the President
Must be a citizen of India
Five years as a High Court judge is one qualification route
A Distinguished Jurist in the President's opinion is another route
No fixed tenure; holds office until 65 years of age
A judge may resign by writing to the President
Removal only on proven misbehaviour or incapacity
Removal by the President on Parliament's recommendation
Judges Enquiry Act, 1968 governs the removal procedure for SC and HC judges

subtopics.title: CJI Appointment Convention and Collegium
subtopics.summary: Until 1973 the seniormost judge was normally appointed Chief Justice of India, a convention that was broken in 1973 and 1977. The Second Judges Case (1993) ruled that only the seniormost judge should be appointed CJI and that consultation means concurrence. The 2015 Fourth Judges Case struck down the NJAC and the 99th Amendment.
facts: Till 1973, the seniormost judge was normally appointed CJI
1973: AN Ray appointed CJI, superseding JM Shelat, KS Hegde and AN Grover
1977: MU Beg appointed CJI, superseding HR Khanna
1981 (First Judges Case): consultation only implies exchange of views
1993 (Second Judges Case): consultation changed to mean concurrence
1993: only the seniormost judge should be appointed CJI
1998 (Third Judges Case): CJI must consult a collegium of 4 seniormost judges
1998: if 2 judges give an adverse opinion, no recommendation is sent
2015 (Fourth Judges Case): 99th Amendment and NJAC Act declared void
NJAC: CJI chairperson, 2 seniormost judges, Law Minister, 2 eminent persons

subtopics.title: Jurisdiction and Temporary Appointments
subtopics.summary: The Supreme Court has appellate, original and advisory jurisdiction. Article 32 allows direct approach for violation of Fundamental Rights, while the President can seek an advisory opinion under Article 143 that is not binding. Articles 126, 127 and 128 allow an Acting CJI, ad hoc judges and retired judges in specified situations.
facts: Appellate jurisdiction covers appeals against lower court judgments
Appeals from High Courts need a certificate under Article 134A
Article 131 gives original jurisdiction in certain disputes
Article 32: direct approach for violation of Fundamental Rights
Article 143: President may seek advisory opinion on public importance questions
Advisory opinion is NOT binding on the President
Article 126: Acting CJI appointed when CJI post is vacant or absent
Article 127: CJI can appoint a High Court judge as ad hoc judge for lack of quorum
Article 127 needs prior consent of the President
Article 128: retired SC or HC judge can be requested to sit, with consent

quizzes.passage: The appointment of judges to the Supreme Court has been a subject of repeated litigation in India, and the Court has ruled on it several times. For a long period after the Court was set up, the seniormost judge of the Supreme Court was generally appointed Chief Justice of India. This practice was set aside twice in the 1970s, when the government chose judges who were not the seniormost. The Constitution requires the President to consult certain persons before appointing judges, and the meaning of the word consultation became a dispute. The First Judges Case of 1981 examined this word. The Second Judges Case of 1993 later revisited the question of how the Chief Justice of India should be chosen. The Third Judges Case of 1998 dealt with the process that the Chief Justice must follow before sending recommendations to the Government. Parliament later sought to replace the collegium with a new body, the National Judicial Appointments Commission, through a constitutional amendment and an Act. The Fourth Judges Case of 2015 examined that amendment and the Act. The rulings are known as the First, Second, Third and Fourth Judges Cases. The 1973 and 1977 appointments were made by the government of the time.

quizzes.passage: Judicial appointments in India have been shaped by a series of decisions over several decades. The Constitution provides that judges of the Supreme Court are appointed by the President, and that the Chief Justice of India is appointed after consultation with judges the President considers necessary. For a long period after the Court was set up, the most senior judge was usually chosen to lead the Court as its head. That pattern was broken twice in the 1970s. Later, the Supreme Court interpreted the word consultation in the context of appointments. The Third Judges Case addressed the steps the Chief Justice must take before advising the government. The Second Judges Case addressed the advice tendered by the Chief Justice and the judges he consults. A proposal to create a National Judicial Appointments Commission was made through a constitutional amendment and an Act of Parliament. The Court examined that amendment and Act in 2015. The cases raised questions about the weight to be given to the Chief Justice's view and about the place of the government in appointments. The rulings are commonly known by their ordinal numbers, such as the First and Second Judges Cases. Each judgment discussed here is known by its year and by the question it addressed.

quizzes.passage: The Supreme Court of India exercises more than one kind of jurisdiction. It hears appeals against decisions of lower courts, decides certain disputes at the first instance, and gives advice when asked. A person whose Fundamental Rights have been violated may approach the Court directly, which gives the Court a role beyond routine appeals. The President of India can also refer questions of public importance to the Court. The Constitution provides for situations in which the Court may need a temporary head or additional judges. One provision deals with the office of the Chief Justice of India when that office is vacant or cannot be filled, while others allow the Chief Justice to draw on judges who are not part of the regular bench. Such provisions are meant for specific circumstances and carry their own conditions. Some of these arrangements involve a retired judge or a High Court judge. The Court's jurisdiction is therefore divided into several parts, each set out in the Constitution. The arrangements described above allow the Court to continue its work when its regular composition is incomplete or its head is unavailable. Each of these provisions is a separate route, and a reader must know which one applies to a given situation.

quizzes.passage: The Supreme Court of India has a few separate routes into its work. Ordinary cases arrive as appeals from lower courts. Some disputes can be filed straight in the Supreme Court because of their nature, such as disputes between the Union and the States. Individuals can also approach the Court directly when their rights are violated. The head of the state may seek the Court's advice on questions of public importance. When the office of the Chief Justice is empty or the Chief Justice cannot act, another judge may take charge. When the Court lacks enough judges to hold a sitting, a High Court judge may be called in temporarily. A retired judge may also be asked to sit for a temporary period. Each of these situations is governed by a specific provision of the Constitution, and the provision must be read with its conditions. The Court's appellate, original and advisory roles together define the scope of its work, and the provisions for temporary arrangements support those roles. Some of these provisions apply to the Chief Justice, while others apply to judges who are not part of the regular bench, and the booklet describes each of them. Each is described with its own conditions.
